## Summary by CodeRabbit

## Walkthrough

This changeset systematically replaces public constructors with controlled factory entry points across many modules. Most classes gain static factory methods (commonly `new`, `fromRaw`, `assemble`, `forService`) and their original constructors are made private/protected. All call sites were updated to use the new factories. No business logic, control flow, or runtime behavior was changed beyond instantiation and constructor visibility adjustments.

💡 Result:

Yes, the JavaScript BigInt64Array constructor requires the byteOffset to be a multiple of 8 (its BYTES_PER_ELEMENT). If not, it throws a RangeError. BigInt64Array is a TypedArray subclass. MDN documentation for TypedArray constructors, including BigInt64Array, states that all TypedArray subclass constructors share the same exceptions and validation rules. Specifically, when constructing from an ArrayBuffer with byteOffset, "the length of buffer (if the length parameter is not specified) or byteOffset is not an integral multiple of the element size" throws RangeError. For BigInt64Array, element size is 8 bytes. MDN explicitly documents: "ByteOffset must be aligned. When constructing a TypedArray as a view onto an ArrayBuffer, the byteOffset argument must be aligned to its element size; in other words, the offset must be a multiple of BYTES_PER_ELEMENT." Example given for Int32Array (offset 1 not multiple of 4) throws RangeError: "start offset of Int32Array should be a multiple of 4". Stack Overflow confirms typed array constructors require offset modulo element size == 0, throwing exception otherwise, due to alignment for performance/portability. ECMAScript specification (2026 draft) links confirm TypedArray constructors perform this validation, throwing RangeError for unaligned byteOffset. TC39 issue discusses the spec requiring "If offset modulo elementSize ≠ 0, throw a RangeError exception." Examples in MDN for BigInt64Array use aligned offsets like 8, which is 8 % 8 == 0.

🌐 Web query:

`In TypeScript, if class B extends class A with a protected constructor and B declares no constructor, can external code call `new B(...)`? Please cite official TypeScript docs/handbook.`

💡 Result:

No, external code cannot call new B(...) if class B extends class A (with a protected constructor) and B declares no constructor. When a derived class does not declare a constructor, TypeScript provides a default public constructor that calls super(...) with the same parameter list as the base class constructor. This default constructor is public (default visibility), allowing external code to call new B(...). However, since the base constructor is protected, the generated super(...) call inside the default constructor is invalid because protected constructors can only be called from within subclasses, not implicitly through the default mechanism. This results in a TypeScript compilation error: "Constructor of class 'A' is protected and only accessible within class 'A' subclasses." External code can attempt new B(...) syntactically, but it won't compile due to the invalid super call. Official TypeScript Handbook confirms protected constructors prevent instantiation outside the class but allow extension, and derived classes typically declare constructors to call super properly (e.g., https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/classes.html#understanding-protected). ESLint rules like no-useless-constructor flag unnecessary constructors in such cases, implying explicit declaration is needed (https://github.com/typescript-eslint/typescript-eslint/issues/8059). Secondary sources note protected constructors enforce subclass-only instantiation via explicit constructors (https://www.codegenes.net/blog/what-is-the-usage-of-private-and-protected-constructors-in-typescript/).

Citations:

- 1: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/classes
- 2: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/classes.html
- 3: https://typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/classes.html
